## TL;DR

A board left open for days was doing continuous work with nothing changing:
every `TaskCard` owned a 15-second `setInterval`, every card's `held`
computed subscribed to the shared one-second clock, `byStatus()` filtered and
sorted the whole task list on every template read, every streamed agent line
rebuilt a transcript record and copied up to 2000 entries, check/test-run logs
grew without a cap, and reconnects ran on a fixed cadence that made every tab
retry in lockstep. The fix makes idle cost structural: no timer exists unless a
card's copy can actually change with time, the clock is shared and stops while
hidden, board columns read a memoised per-status cache, log buffers are capped,
and the SSE client owns a jittered exponential reconnect. Measured idle
main-thread cost on a 200–300-card fixture fell from ~7–10% of one core with
~14 timer callbacks/s to ~1.6–2% flat with no per-card timers.

## Work and rationale

I started from the report's strongest signals: the renderer and GPU processes
were both busy for days, memory reached ~640 MB, and killing them fixed the
host. That pattern fits per-card work multiplied by hundreds of cards plus
unbounded buffers, not one slow handler.

The largest structural cost was `TaskCard`'s timer. It existed only to refresh
a `now` ref used for live state — stuck-agent age, integration elapsed,
countdowns — but was created for every card at mount. Hundreds of intervals,
all started together, meant a burst of full card re-renders every 15 seconds
forever. `needsNowTick()` now gates it on state that genuinely changes with
time, and the timer stops while the document is hidden and resyncs on return.

The second cost was subscription amplification. A card with no hold still read
`holdNow` inside its `held` computed, so the one-second clock invalidated
hundreds of computeds for no possible change. `taskIsHeld()` now short-circuits
before the clock read in `TaskCard`, `TaskDrawer`, and `heldTasks`, and
`useNow` itself is visibility-aware: one timer, stopped while hidden, advanced
once on return.

`byStatus()` became a computed cache grouped once per `tasks`/`sortOrder`
change. Its public signature is unchanged, so `BoardColumn`'s repeated template
reads are now O(1) instead of filtering and sorting hundreds of tasks several
times per repaint.

Streamed output was the memory story. Transcript appends now push and trim in
place; check runs are capped at 25 per task, a single check's output at 400 KB,
the full test-suite output at 500 KB, and the agent-activity map is mutated in
place rather than spread per line.

For the server, `EventSource`'s built-in retry made every tab reconnect at the
same instant after a restart, and each reconnect pulled the full index. The
board client now closes the stream and reconnects with exponential backoff from
1 s to 30 s with full jitter (reset on a real open), and the server's `retry:`
hint is itself jittered 1–3 s for other consumers.

Finally, visibility is honoured everywhere: App.vue toggles a class that pauses
CSS animations/transitions, pollers skip their request while hidden, and
`system.stats` is not applied to the store while nothing is visible.

## Approaches tried

I built the app and drove the built UI in headless Chromium through
Playwright/CDP against generated fixture repos, sampling `TaskDuration`,
`ScriptDuration`, DOM mutations (MutationObserver), rAF callbacks, request
counts and heap. I measured the pre-fix branch by checking out its detached
HEAD into a temporary worktree with the same fixture. Headless Chromium cannot
set a page hidden via CDP, so hidden-tab behaviour is pinned by fake-timer unit
tests with a stubbed `visibilityState` instead of a browser sample.

## Challenges and blockers

The real incident's 97% CPU and 640 MB over 1.5 days cannot be reproduced in a
short run: headless Chromium does not expose GPU/compositor metrics, and heap
peaks depend on streaming volume. The evidence is therefore the proven
mechanisms (timer census, mutation rate, buffer caps) plus a short-run before/
after, with the maintainer's incident numbers as the long-run evidence. PWA and
tab are the same app and renderer; the PWA was only where it was noticed, and a
visible standalone window keeps animations running where a minimized tab would
be throttled.

## Key learnings

Per-card timers are the trap: cost scales with board size and never idles.
Subscribe to a clock only when time can change the output. Bound every streamed
buffer at the write site. Reconnect jitter belongs in the client, not only in a
server hint. And measure idle cost structurally (timers, mutations, caps) when
wall-clock cannot represent a multi-day leak.
